content: The guidelines for managing patients with Chagas disease adhere to the GRADE methodology, providing evidence-based recommendations for healthcare professionals. The document is structured into several parts: 1. Theoretical Framework: This section outlines the scope, objectives, and target population of the guidelines. It provides a foundational understanding of the purpose and intended use of the recommendations. 2. Methodology: The methodology used to develop the guidelines is described in detail. This includes the processes for formulating clinical questions, identifying and grading outcomes, and conducting systematic reviews of the evidence. 3. Clinical Questions and Recommendations: Specific clinical questions are posed, and evidence-based recommendations are provided to address them. These recommendations are supported by the panel’s judgments and are categorized based on the quality of evidence and strength of recommendation using the GRADE system. 4. Implementation and Updates: Strategies for updating and implementing the guidelines are discussed to ensure their continued relevance and applicability in clinical practice. 5. Supplementary Information: Additional details on the guideline development process are included, such as the PICO questions, evidence summaries, subgroup analyses, and tables assessing the validity of surrogate outcomes. A list of the development group members is also provided. Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a neglected tropical disease that poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Despite its endemic nature in the Americas, clinical suspicion and diagnosis are infrequent, even in high-risk areas. This is largely due to insufficient training and awareness among healthcare providers, as well as difficulties in accessing and interpreting laboratory tests. The guidelines aim to address these gaps by providing clear indications for the diagnosis and treatment of Chagas disease. They are intended for use by healthcare professionals, including pediatricians, general practitioners, family doctors, gynecologists, and obstetricians, as well as decision-makers and government agencies involved in public health. Chagas disease is a chronic systemic parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. It is primarily transmitted by hematophagous triatomine insects but can also spread through blood transfusions, organ transplants, and vertical transmission. While prevention and control measures have reduced the incidence and prevalence of the disease, significant challenges remain in providing timely and appropriate care. Only about 1% of infected individuals receive proper diagnosis and treatment each year, highlighting the need for improved healthcare access and education. The guidelines were developed by a multidisciplinary group of experts, including thematic specialists, epidemiologists, and methodologists. The process involved formulating clinical questions using the PICO format, conducting systematic reviews of the literature, and prioritizing outcomes based on their significance to patients. The recommendations are categorized by the quality of evidence (high, moderate, low, or very low) and the strength of recommendation (strong or conditional) according to the GRADE system. The development group ensured transparency and independence throughout the process. All members declared the absence of conflicts of interest, and the guidelines were designed to provide equitable, efficient, and high-quality care for individuals affected by Chagas disease. The document serves as a reference to promote technical and scientific collaboration in the diagnosis and treatment of this condition across the Americas and beyond.
